title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Using Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation, two deterministic validators combined with a logical-OR decision rule, and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms), we completed all planned episodes (600) with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0); McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because validators never reported forbidden reachability, the repair step was never invoked and the study cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. We present a compact technical definition of the forbidden-reachability predicate and each validator's detection assumptions, a concise numeric Results table, and an artifact-verification paragraph pointing to the archived evidence bundle for reproducibility. The primary empirical contribution is deterministic execution accounting, transparent artifacts, and design lessons for follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths.

sections.introduction: LLM-driven intent→configuration translation promises operational efficiency for network operators but raises legitimate safety concerns: incorrectly generated configurations can expand attack surface, violate access-control constraints, or otherwise introduce security-regressions. Prior system and survey work therefore emphasizes constrained generation and verifier-assisted iterative repair (GVR) as operational mitigations [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898; https://openalex.org/W4415071524]. We ask a focused operational question and answer it under a preregistered, deterministic experimental contract: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven pipeline when exposed to a matched set of benign and programmatic adversarial intents? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) executed deterministically on Dockerized emulation; (2) a concise, artifact-grounded quantification of outcomes for N = 300 matched intents under a shared_initial_candidate contract; (3) a clear statement of the trial's principal limitation—repair was never exercised because no validator-detected violations occurred—and practical design recommendations that follow directly from the archived accounting; and (4) the full set of execution and analysis artifacts archived for reproducibility.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures improve correctness in code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repairs; TerraFormer and related work demonstrate verifier-driven gains for infrastructure artifacts but highlight dependence on verifier power and repair design [doi:10.1145/3786583.3786898]. Surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and recommend validators, constrained generation, and human oversight [https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4404602270]. Emulation and testbed work show execution-based validation is feasible for research evaluation, while noting transportability limits to production environments [https://openalex.org/W4406170828]. Our study complements these works by providing a preregistered, paired, execution-validated experiment that explicitly records the consequences of a generation-cost trade-off (shared vs independent generation) on the ability to exercise repair.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The preregistered design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary confirmatory test on N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds, each paired with one programmatic adversarial variant). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). Primary test: exact McNemar two-sided (alpha = 0.05). CIs: bootstrap percentile; final analysis used 10,000 resamples (seed 1729) as recorded in the analysis log.

Adapter contract and generation semantics: To bound provider usage we executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate generated per paired intent and replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This produced model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs (provider-call accounting archived). The guarded arm allowed up to one repair LLM call only when a validator reported forbidden reachability; repairs were therefore conditional on validator-detected violations.

Technical definition: forbidden-reachability predicate and validators. Forbidden-reachability (operationalized in scoring) marks a configuration as violating if any validator reports that the final network state enables reachability that is disallowed by per-task policy constraints. Per-task policy constraints are encoded in each task's payload (for example, 'protected_interfaces' such as mgmt1 and workflow_policies in task_manifest entries) and include forbidden-exposure conditions (e.g., new reachability to protected interfaces or violations of required workflow order). Two deterministic validators were used (both run in Docker): (1) an execution-based Batfish-style validator that applies the generated configuration in the FRRouting-style emulator and issues concrete reachability queries against the emulated dataplane (captures dynamics, run-time forwarding behaviors, and observable ECMP), and (2) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer implemented in Python that evaluates reachability on an abstracted configuration graph (fast, deterministic, may miss dynamic or policy-dependent behaviors). Scoring combined the two validators with a logical OR: a configuration is labeled violating if either validator reports forbidden reachability. Known limitations: the execution validator's judgments depend on emulator fidelity (control-/data-plane modeling) and the static analyzer can produce false negatives on configurations that require path-dependent semantics or complex route-policy evaluation. Per-episode validator traces and task policy encodings are archived for inspection.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed episodes = 600; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300. The run interval and provider-call audit are archived in the execution manifest.

Primary outcomes (compact):

- N (complete matched pairs) = 300
- baseline_success_count = 300 (no forbidden-reachability detected)
- guarded_success_count = 300 (no forbidden-reachability detected)
- Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0
- Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0
- McNemar exact two-sided p-value = 1.0
- Bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]
- One-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on baseline violation rate ≈ 0.00994

Because validators never flagged forbidden reachability for any initial candidate, the preregistered repair policy was never invoked (repair_applied = false for every archived validator_trace). Consequently, the experiment tests whether inserting a verifier changes compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract; it does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating outputs. Representative per-task responses and per-episode validator_trace files (examples included among archived artifacts) show consistent parsing, normalization, and 'valid=true' judgments from the validators. Full per-episode raw responses, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis tables (paired contingency and condition summary) are archived for verification.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: The degenerate contingency (all pairs concordant-pass) is directly attributable to two coupled design choices: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics reduced independent-sample variability between arms (exact one LLM generation per pair), and (2) under the chosen model and validator set the programmatic adversarial perturbations did not produce validator-detectable forbidden-reachability. Together these factors prevented any repair activity and rendered the paired McNemar test uninformative for assessing repair efficacy.

Operational lessons and recommendations: (a) Generation semantics are an experimental lever: independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) increases the chance of producing discordant violating outputs but doubles model-call budget; archived provider-call accounting documents this trade-off. (b) Adversary design must be tuned to predicate/validator weaknesses: stronger or targeted adversaries may be required to exercise repair. (c) Verifier diversity and oracle strength matter: combining different oracle families and including production-grade dynamic oracles can expose predicate-specific failure modes. (d) Reproducible accounting is practical: all raw responses, validator traces, and the provider-call audit are archived to enable deterministic replay and targeted stress tests.

Threats to validity (brief): Internal validity limited by shared_initial_candidate and single-model scope; construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and two deterministic validators capture operational security risk; external validity limited by synthetic tasks and Dockerized emulation; conclusion validity constrained because the observed contingency violated preregistered power assumptions. Artifact locations for these claims are recorded in the evidence bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline (declared model: gpt-5-mini) under a shared_initial_candidate contract. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised; therefore the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair rescues violating outputs. The primary empirical value is deterministic execution accounting, open artifacts, and explicit design lessons: choice of generation semantics, adversary potency, repair budget, and verifier strength materially affect whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise repair paths (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.

Model and verifier scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
